newsitem.title: FRANCE: Toubon defends new, tougher anti-racism laws.
newsitem.headline: Toubon defends new, tougher anti-racism laws.

text.p: French Justice Minister Jacques Toubon on Thursday defended a draft bill to toughen anti-racism laws, denying it threatened basic freedoms or was an effort to silence extreme right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen.

Toubon unveiled plans to stiffen legislation after Le Pen, whose National Front party proposes sending immigrants home, said racial inequality was "a fact". Toubon said the remarks could not be prosecuted under existing laws.

"This bill does not exclusively target the National Front, or only racism against foreigners or immigrants," Toubon said in an interview with the daily Le Figaro. "It is the fruit of long philosophical and technical reflection."
Critics in the opposition as well as the ruling centre-right coalition have said the bill threatens freedom of speech, on issues including religion and patriotism.
"The bill in no way infringes on basic freedoms," said Tooubon. "We know from practice how insufficient and difficult it is to apply existing laws."
"Maybe this kind of bill should have been drawn up 25 years ago. But circumstances are more serious today with the undeniable rise of racist acts...and the rise of intolerance," he said.

Toubon, who hopes to put the legislation before the National Assembly at the start of its autumn session next month, has submitted it to the National Consultative Human Rights Committee, which will give its opinion later on Thursday.

The bill would make anyone making a racist statement in public liable to one year in prison and a 300,000 franc ($60,000) fine. Sanctions would increase to two years in jail and a 500,000 franc ($100,000) fine if the remark were judged an incitement to discrimination, hate or violence.

The bill also widens the scope of existing legislation to include statements aimed at "an ethnic group, a nation, a race or a religion" and lengthens the statute of limitations, currently at three months, to one year.
Meanwhile, several Leftist movements, including the Socialist and Communist parties, met to discuss a common strategy to fight racism and prevent the National Front from gaining popularity.
They were considering forming a racism vigilance committee or proposing alternative legislation.
Le Pen, who in the past dismissed the Nazi gas chambers as a mere detail in the history of World War Two, won 15 percent in 1995 presidential elections.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe last week branded Le Pen "deeply, almost viscerally racist, anti-Semitic and xenophobic".
In the run up to 1998 legislative election, the centre-right government feels threatened by the Front which exploits worries about unemployment and growing insecurity.
